text: Two small but easy-to-trip-on details to wrap up this chapter: how comments work, and how statements end. One of these is identical everywhere. The other, plus a tooling quirk called GO, genuinely differs across platforms.

Good news first — comments are the same everywhere. Double-dash for a single line, slash-star star-slash for a block comment, on T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL alike. Zero divergence here, which is rare in this course.

Statement terminators are where it gets interesting. T-SQL has historically let you skip the semicolon for most single statements — but that's shifting. Newer syntax, like common table expressions, actually requires a semicolon before the WITH keyword that starts them, which is part of why semicolons are now broadly recommended in T-SQL even where they're not strictly mandatory.

Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL all effectively require the semicolon, especially the moment a script has more than one statement in it — without it, the parser has no way to know where one statement ends and the next one starts.

And then there's GO — which is not SQL at all. It's a signal that SQL Server Management Studio and sqlcmd understand, telling the TOOL to send everything since the last GO as one batch. The database engine itself never sees it. Paste GO into Oracle's SQL asterisk Plus, or PostgreSQL's psql, and you'll get a syntax error, because neither tool has any idea what it means. One lesson left in this chapter: a full side-by-side of string functions across all four dialects.
